title: SeaSPRITE — Wireless Surface Vessel Control
problem: A legacy wired joystick limited mobility and classroom flexibility.
goal: Build an affordable, modular wireless controller capable of at least 50 meters of reliable operation.
solution: Led a three-person team integrating two ESP32 controllers, Wi-Fi command transmission, DC motor drive and servo steering. Supported electrical wiring, prototype troubleshooting, system verification and documentation.
result: Reliable land-based communication at approximately 60 ± 5 meters, exceeding the 50-meter target; intermittent performance near 90 meters. Over-water validation remained future work.
description: I led a three-person team developing a remotely operated surface vessel as a senior capstone mentored by the Naval Surface Warfare Center Philadelphia Division. The project required integration of propulsion, steering, electrical power distribution, and wireless control. I worked with an ESP32-based control architecture and developed schematics and test plans to support integration. I assembled and tested prototypes, diagnosed electrical and control issues, and coordinated technical documentation and team progress. The experience strengthened my systems integration, troubleshooting, and engineering leadership skills.

title: PLC & Industrial Automation
problem: Industrial equipment requires predictable and testable sequencing and safe control of electrical inputs and outputs.
goal: Program and verify PLC logic, analog signal monitoring, and motor speed control.
solution: Built and troubleshot Allen-Bradley Micro820 training exercises in Connected Components Workbench; implemented ladder logic, timers, digital/analog I/O and VFD fan speed control.
result: Tested control logic, voltage thresholds and potentiometer-driven speed references on training hardware.
description: I designed, wired, programmed, and troubleshot Allen-Bradley Micro820 PLC training systems at Temple University. Using Connected Components Workbench, I developed ladder logic for digital I/O, relay logic, timers, counters, and sequential operations. I also used analog signals, comparisons, MOV instructions, and voltage thresholds to control indicator outputs. Another exercise integrated a variable frequency drive with pushbutton start-stop controls and potentiometer-based speed regulation. This work built practical skills in industrial control wiring, PLC testing, motor control, and troubleshooting.

title: Construction Materials Testing
problem: Construction teams need verified material properties and documented compliance with specifications.
goal: Support field QA/QC across active construction sites.
solution: Performed soil density and compaction testing, fresh-concrete slump and air-content tests, and rebar/formwork inspections; documented observations and coordinated with site personnel.
result: Produced inspection and testing records supporting construction quality verification.
description: During my field technician internship at Hillis-Carnes Engineering Associates, I tested soil, concrete, and asphalt on active construction projects. I used specialized equipment to collect measurements relevant to compaction, material properties, and project specifications. I also interpreted CAD drawings and inspected rebar placement and formwork before concrete pours. I documented test results and communicated findings to engineers and construction teams. The experience reinforced the importance of field safety, accurate measurements, and dependable engineering documentation.

title: CNC-Milled Bottle Opener
problem: Convert a functional part concept into repeatable machining instructions and a physical component.
goal: Design, program and manufacture a precision bottle opener.
solution: Prepared AutoCAD drawings, generated Mastercam toolpaths for facing, drilling, pocketing and contouring, and applied CNC G-code.
result: Produced a physical metal bottle opener and documented its CAD/CAM workflow.
description: I designed and manufactured a functional bottle opener as a CAD/CAM/CNC project. I produced two-dimensional geometry in AutoCAD and prepared machining operations in Mastercam. I established work coordinates and developed toolpaths for facing, drilling, pocketing, and contouring. I generated and adjusted G-code instructions for the CNC manufacturing process. The project connected digital drafting and toolpath planning with fabrication of a physical part.

title: CNC-Turned Bishop Chess Piece
problem: A rotationally symmetric chess piece requires dimensional planning and careful turning operations.
goal: Model and machine a bishop chess piece using a CNC lathe.
solution: Configured Aluminum 6061 stock, created geometry and machining origins, simulated turning paths in Mastercam and generated G-code.
result: Fabricated a physical aluminum bishop chess piece.
description: I designed and manufactured a bishop chess piece using CNC turning techniques. I developed the geometry in AutoCAD and prepared machining coordinates and operations in Mastercam. The project used Aluminum 6061 as the workpiece material. I programmed and simulated lathe toolpaths to review tool motion before machining. The finished exercise developed my understanding of CNC turning, simulation, material selection, and precision manufacturing.

title: Electric Vehicle Fleet Conversion Study
problem: Replacing a gasoline fleet involves large upfront costs and uncertain operating savings.
goal: Evaluate the economic and environmental feasibility of replacing eight university vehicles with EVs.
solution: Built Excel NPV, after-tax cash-flow, break-even and sensitivity models, including 1,000-trial Monte Carlo analysis.
result: Model projected $493,116 positive NPV, 3.94-year payback and annual CO₂ reduction from 451 to 50 metric tons; scenario estimates, not realized savings.
description: I completed an engineering economic feasibility analysis exploring a potential transition from gasoline vehicles to an electric fleet. The study considered the tradeoffs between initial investment and operating costs. I organized assumptions and compared alternative scenarios to support a reasoned decision. The analysis emphasized the importance of clearly communicating uncertainty and long-term costs. This was an analytical study rather than a physical vehicle conversion.

title: Sooper Dooper Looper
problem: A marble needs sufficient energy to travel through a vertical loop.
goal: Design a functional 3D-printed track informed by kinematics.
solution: Modeled track geometry in SolidWorks, calculated minimum release height and velocity with a 1.3 safety factor, and prepared PLA prints using Cura.
result: Created a track prototype and motion-analysis workflow.
description: I designed a three-dimensional marble-loop track to explore energy conservation and rotational motion. I calculated the release height and velocity required for a steel marble to complete a vertical loop, including a design safety factor. I modeled the track in SolidWorks using sketches, helix geometry, and sweep features. I reviewed motion behavior and prepared the model for additive manufacturing. I exported the design to STL and configured Cura for a PLA 3D-printed prototype.

title: Secure Web Application
problem: Account-based applications need organized authentication and user-data workflows.
goal: Develop a database-backed web application with registration, login and password reset.
solution: Collaborated on an MVC application and MySQL relational database, integrating interactive account-management pages.
result: Delivered academic application functionality for account registration and authentication.
description: I collaborated on a secure web application organized around the Model-View-Controller architecture. The project included account registration, login, authentication, and password-reset workflows. I helped implement a MySQL relational database to store and manage user information. The team connected responsive web interfaces with database-backed functionality. This experience introduced me to structured application development and collaborative software design.

title: Automatic Night Light Circuit
problem: An LED should respond to ambient light using an analog sensing circuit.
goal: Design and analyze a photoresistor-controlled night light.
solution: Applied Wheatstone bridge, voltage divider and Thevenin analysis; modeled behavior in NI Multisim.
result: Developed and simulated a circuit targeting a 2 V, 20 mA LED.
description: I developed an automatic night-light circuit concept using a photoresistor and LED. The design explored how changes in ambient light could produce an electrical response. I applied Ohm's Law, Kirchhoff's Laws, voltage dividers, Thevenin's theorem, and Wheatstone bridge analysis. I used NI Multisim to simulate resistance changes and evaluate circuit behavior. The project strengthened my DC circuit analysis and simulation skills.

title: AC Filter Design
problem: Electronic systems need selective frequency response and signal conditioning.
goal: Analyze low-pass and high-pass filters against specified cutoff targets.
solution: Developed circuit models and transfer-function analysis, examining 1.54 kHz and 72.34 kHz targets with ±5% tolerance.
result: Evaluated filter response and amplifier design options using circuit simulation.
description: I designed and analyzed low-pass and high-pass AC filters against specified frequency-response requirements. The project used circuit theory, complex impedance, and transfer functions to understand attenuation and cutoff behavior. I investigated passive filters and active filter modifications involving operational amplifiers. I used NI Multisim and MATLAB-based analysis to compare theoretical and simulated behavior. The work developed my understanding of analog signal conditioning and verification against design specifications.

title: Water Infrastructure Design — Peru
problem: Communities in Lobitos and Piedritas face challenges accessing reliable clean water.
solution: Used weighted multi-criteria assessment to evaluate treatment facilities, storage and pumping, and rainwater collection.
result: Recommended rainwater collection as the highest-scoring conceptual alternative (64).
description: I collaborated with a three-member team on a conceptual water-infrastructure design challenge focused on Lobitos and Piedritas, Peru. We evaluated water treatment, local storage and pumping, and rainwater collection alternatives. Using a weighted multi-criteria assessment in Microsoft Excel, we compared social, economic, environmental, and implementation factors. Rainwater collection stations received the highest score in our conceptual comparison. The project taught me to evaluate engineering alternatives while considering community needs and practical constraints.

title: Portable Liver Transport System
problem: Organ transportation requires careful preservation and system reliability.
goal: Investigate design constraints and risk-reduction concepts for donor-liver transport.
solution: Researched perfusion approaches, stakeholder requirements, power and pump failure modes, and redundant-system concepts.
result: Produced conceptual reliability recommendations; not a clinically validated device.
description: I collaborated on an engineering design research project examining safer transportation and preservation of donor livers. The team researched conventional cold storage and normothermic machine perfusion concepts. We identified stakeholder needs and constraints involving transport duration, power supply, equipment size, and reliability. We assessed potential hazards such as power overload and pump failure and considered redundant systems. The project was a conceptual research and design exercise, not a clinically validated medical device.
